sentences.text: Her grandfather's watch was in the wall, third row, near the left-hand passage, and she saw it on the second visit and said so out loud in a voice that came out wrong, and the badger did not give it to her.
That was November.
She spent from November to March trying to get it.
She would like to be clear that the badger never refused her and never drove her off.
It did not hide the watch or block the row.

On perhaps half her visits it would take the watch out of the wall itself, without being asked, and put it on the floor between them and sit there — and if she reached for it, it would put a paw on it, and that was all, and there was never any question of a struggle.
She tried asking.
She tried asking politely.
She tried explaining, at length, out loud, in a hole in the ground, that it was hers, that it had been her grandfather's, that he had died in April, and that she wanted it back.
The badger listened to all of it every time — it always listened, it never once went away while she was talking — and did not give her the watch.
In January she brought a photograph of her grandfather, which she now finds embarrassing.
In February she got angry and said a number of things she regretted on the walk home.

In the first week of March she came in wet and cold and out of ideas and sat down on the floor of the chamber and said, "I don't know what you want." And the badger came over and put one claw on the floor and drew her grandfather's entry, slowly, twice, and then sat back.
Orla looked at it for a long time.
It was seven strokes.
She could not read it.

But she had by then spent four months watching that animal draw entries, and she had understood some time in February — without being able to prove it, and without ever telling anybody, because there is no way to say it that does not sound mad — that the entries were not descriptions of objects.
Seven strokes was not *a watch*.
Seven strokes was whatever the watch had been doing, on the ninth of October, on the wrist of an eleven-year-old girl in a wood.
And Orla, sitting on the floor with her back against the earth, realised that she did not know.
She knew what the watch was.
She did not know what it had been doing.
She did not know why it had stopped in 2011 and she did not know why he had gone on wearing it stopped for fourteen years, and she had never asked him, and she was not going to be able to now.
